paper_metadata.title: Quantum Quantile Mechanics: Solving Stochastic Diﬀerential Equations for Generating Time-Series

summary: The paper proposes Quantum Quantile Mechanics (QQM), a variational quantum algorithm using 6‑qubit differentiable quantum circuits to learn and time‑evolve the quantile function of stochastic differential equations. Experiments on the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process use a 6‑qubit HEA circuit with 21 latent grid points and 20 time points, and sampling evaluations with 100,000 generated samples. All results are produced on a noiseless Yao.jl statevector simulator and show qualitative agreement with analytic distributions and Euler–Maruyama simulations.

experiments.description: Quantum quantile mechanics (QQM) training of a differentiable quantum circuit to represent and time-evolve the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck quantile function from an analytic initial condition, followed by sampling and comparison to Euler-Maruyama.

algorithm.variant: quantum quantile mechanics with differentiable quantum circuits (DQC) and feature-map encoding
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA) with six layers of generic single-qubit rotations plus nearest-neighbor CNOTs
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed number of epochs; training loss reported after convergence

hyperparameters.feature_maps: U_phi(t)=⊗_j exp[-i arcsin(t) Y_j/2], U_phi'(z)=⊗_j exp[-i arcsin(z) X_j/2]

algorithm.parameter_initialization: not specified for this experiment; analytic initial condition G(z,0)=Q(z,0) used

problem_formulation.encoding_details: latent variable z and time t encoded via product feature maps using arcsin rotations on each qubit
problem_formulation.objective_function: learn quantile function Q(z,t) satisfying quantile-mechanics PDE for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; minimize L = L_data + L_SDE, with L_SDE based on mismatch between ∂G/∂t and the quantile PDE RHS
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: floating boundary handling for initial condition; differential constraint via quantile-mechanics equation

problem_instance.description: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic process for time-series generation and financial forecasting

dataset_specification.preprocessing: analytic initial delta distribution evolved under OU; samples drawn from trained quantile and Euler-Maruyama reference

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: analytic initial condition p(x,t0)=δ(x-x0); samples binned and normalized for histogram comparison
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: compare sampled histograms from QQM against analytic PDF and Euler-Maruyama using 100,000 samples

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; Euler-Maruyama used as classical reference baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: histogram binning and sorting for quantile training
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sample histograms compared to analytic PDF and Euler-Maruyama

speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit speedup claim or complexity advantage is quantified for this experiment; the paper only reports qualitative agreement with Euler-Maruyama and analytic PDFs.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: unknown; no fault‑tolerant resource estimates provided
limiting_factors: Demonstrated only on a 6‑qubit noiseless simulator
No complexity comparison to classical SDE solvers
No runtime benchmarking against classical methods
Sampling and training evaluated only on small toy Ornstein–Uhlenbeck instance

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states a full quantum state simulator in a noiseless setting and names Yao.jl, with no real QPU device.
Speedup order is not characterized in the paper; set to none_proven.
The paper motivates potential advantages of quantum sampling but does not claim or demonstrate a concrete computational speedup over classical SDE solvers.

experiments.description: QQM training of a differentiable quantum circuit to infer the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck initial quantile function from data, then propagate it in time and sample at later times.

algorithm.variant: quantum quantile mechanics with data-inferred initial condition and time propagation
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA) with six layers of generic single-qubit rotations plus nearest-neighbor CNOTs
algorithm.convergence_criteria: loss around 10^-6 for initial quantile fit; then time-propagation training

hyperparameters.feature_map: tower-type product feature map U_phi'(z)=⊗_j exp[-i arcsin(z) j Z_j/2]

algorithm.parameter_initialization: pre-training with product states mentioned as reducing epochs; initialization layers optionally used

optimizer_settings.max_iterations: few thousand epochs for initial fit; exact count not specified

problem_formulation.encoding_details: latent variable z encoded via tower feature map; initial data sorted into ascending order and fit on Chebyshev grid points
problem_formulation.objective_function: learn initial quantile function G(z,0) from observed samples, then evolve under quantile-mechanics PDE
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: floating boundary handling; data-based loss plus differential constraint during propagation

problem_instance.description: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with data-inferred initial condition for time-series generation

dataset_specification.preprocessing: samples binned, sorted in ascending order, interpolated; Chebyshev grid points selected

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: ordered samples into bins; interpolated curve from 100,000 samples; 43 Chebyshev points used for training
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: compare learned initial quantile to target, then compare sampled histograms at later times to analytic PDF

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; classical regression used for initialization; Euler-Maruyama as reference baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: sorting and interpolation of observed samples; Chebyshev-grid selection of training points

speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit speedup claim is made; the paper reports accurate data-driven quantile fitting and later-time sampling, but no runtime or complexity comparison.

limiting_factors: Classical preprocessing dominates (sorting and interpolation of 100k samples)
No empirical runtime comparison to classical generative models or SDE solvers
Accuracy evaluated only on a simple OU process

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states a full quantum state simulator in a noiseless setting and names Yao.jl, with no real QPU device.
Speedup order is not characterized in the paper; set to none_proven.
Authors present the method as a generative modeling approach for NISQ devices but provide no quantitative advantage claim or benchmark against classical ML models.

experiments.description: Continuous qGAN training to model a normal distribution for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fixed-time sampling task, including generator/discriminator training and reordered-quantile analysis.

algorithm.variant: continuous qGAN / variational quantum generator with feature-map encoding
algorithm.ansatz: expressive Chebyshev tower feature map followed by d=6 HEA ansatz
algorithm.convergence_criteria: generator/discriminator losses near Nash equilibrium; best model selected when |L_G-L_D|<0.1 and minimal KS distance

hyperparameters.target_distribution: normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.2

problem_formulation.encoding_details: continuous latent variable z in [-1,1] encoded by feature map; generator output interpreted as quantile-like function
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimax GAN objective LGAN = min_G max_D [E_x log D(x) + E_z log(1-D(G(z)))]
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: adversarial training; KS test used only for model selection, not training

problem_instance.description: Fixed-time generation of a normal distribution used as a proxy for OU sampling

dataset_specification.preprocessing: target normal distribution with μ=0, σ=0.2

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: not specified beyond target distribution definition
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: loss oscillation around Nash equilibrium; histogram comparison; KS test to choose best epoch

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; KS test for model selection
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: ordering of latent variable values for quantile analysis
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: reordering qGAN output into monotonic quantile function for analysis

speedup_claims.caveats: The qGAN is compared qualitatively against QQM, but no explicit speedup over a classical method is quantified. The paper emphasizes that qGAN training is oscillatory and requires KS-based model selection.

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states a full quantum state simulator in a noiseless setting and names Yao.jl, with no real QPU device.
Speedup order is not characterized in the paper; set to none_proven.

experiments.description: Continuous quantum generative adversarial network (qGAN) trained to reproduce a normal distribution for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck sampling task and compared via histogram statistics and reordered quantile analysis.

algorithm.variant: continuous qGAN with quantum generator and discriminator
algorithm.ansatz: Chebyshev tower feature map followed by hardware-efficient ansatz
algorithm.model_selection: best model chosen when |L_G − L_D| < 0.1 and Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance to data is minimal

key_results: Generator trained for 2000 epochs to model a normal distribution (μ=0, σ=0.2).
Sampling evaluation performed with Ns = 100,000 generated samples.
Resulting generator approximates the distribution but shows missing tails and oscillatory generator function.
Reordered quantile function approximately matches the true quantile but with visible deviations, especially in the tails.
